p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text follows a popular claim – that music can sharpen an older mind – through a study, and ends with its own verdict: what an older learner takes up may matter far less than whether they keep at it. C sums up that verdict. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text. The right answer must cover the main line of the argument, not one study result or one person’s view.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph sets out the popular claim that taking up music can sharpen an older mind, and says that a proper test has been missing. The second reports something close to such a test: older beginners learned the cello, and most of those who practised regularly made small gains. The third adds a group of book-club readers who improved by about as much. The fourth gives one expert’s enthusiasm, and the fifth gives the writer’s verdict.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The last paragraph says: “They suggest that what an older learner takes up may matter far less than whether they keep at it — week after week, in company, at the ragged edge of their own competence.” It ends: “The instrument is optional. The effort is not.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches the verdict: the gains come from keeping at something hard, not from music as such. A makes the cello the best method, B moves the subject to music learned in childhood, and D claims that research proves something about how slowly the brain loses its plasticity.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about where late-life gains come from: steady effort, not music in particular. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The cello is at the centre of the study, and the text opens with the popular story that taking up an instrument sharpens an older mind.
distractors.why_wrong: The book-club readers improved by roughly the same margin as the cellists, and the text concludes that whatever lifted the scores “did not appear to be music as such”. A makes the cello the most effective method, which the text never says (steps 2–3).

distractors.why_tempting: The first paragraph mentions studies of lifelong musicians, so a claim about music learned early can seem to belong to the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text questions those studies, because the musicians “may have differed in a dozen quiet ways from the start”. Its own evidence comes from beginners aged sixty-eight and over, and it never claims that training begun in childhood brings benefits in old age.

distractors.why_tempting: In the fourth paragraph Pellerham says that the mind of an older person is “far more plastic than we once believed” – that is, more able to change – so a claim about plasticity can seem to come from the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The nearest thing in the text is Pellerham’s opinion, not a research result. The text never says that any research proves how slowly the brain loses its plasticity, and its own verdict is about effort, not plasticity (step 3).

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions, read the opening and the closing paragraphs first. Here the opening sets up a popular claim and the closing gives the writer’s verdict on it; the right answer states the verdict, not a single result or a quoted opinion.
p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not pick the most memorable image. The cello fills much of the text, but the text uses it to reach a different point: the effort matters more than the instrument.

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The second paragraph says that most of the volunteers who practised regularly made modest gains of a few percent, and that the gains were still there three months later. A says the same. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about one group: the volunteers “who practiced regularly”. The answer must be stated in the text, so find the sentence about that group in the second paragraph.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “Most of those who practiced regularly showed measurable improvements, modest ones, on the order of a few percent — and, encouragingly, the gains were still there when the same people were tested three months later.”

steps.title: Note the size and the timing
steps.text: Two facts matter. The gains were small – “modest ones, on the order of a few percent” – and they lasted: they were still there three months later. The right option needs both.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A keeps both facts. It leaves out “Most”, but unlike B it does not claim that every volunteer improved. B makes the gains dramatic and gives them to every participant, C invents a practice time far above the text’s figure, and D compares older and younger beginners, which the text never does.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Most of those who practised regularly made small gains that lasted. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The result is good news, and B sounds like an enthusiastic way of reporting it.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says “Most”, not every participant, and calls the improvements “modest ones, on the order of a few percent” (step 2). B turns a small gain for most into a dramatic gain for all.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does give a figure for practice time, and a demanding course can sound as if it took many hours a week.
distractors.why_wrong: The only practice figure in the text is “a little under three hours of practice a week” on average for those who stayed. Nothing in the text comes near ten hours.

distractors.why_tempting: It sounds like the kind of general finding that a study of older learners might report.
distractors.why_wrong: Every volunteer was at least sixty-eight, and the text never compares older beginners with younger ones, on string instruments or anything else.

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “What are we told about …” questions, find the sentence about the named group and check each option against it. Watch the amount words: “Most” and “modest” rule out an option with “Every” and “dramatically”.
p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: An option can keep the right topic and change the amounts. B turns “Most” into “Every” and “modest” into “dramatically”, and a quick reader can miss both.

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The third paragraph says that the book-club readers’ attention scores climbed by roughly the same margin as the cellists’ scores. D says the same in other words. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the comparison group showed. That group is described in the third paragraph: volunteers of the same age and from the same town who joined a demanding book club instead of learning the cello.

steps.title: Find the result
steps.text: The result is in one sentence: “Yet when their attention scores came back, they had climbed by roughly the same margin as the cellists'.”

steps.title: Put it in plain words
steps.text: “Roughly the same margin” means that the readers improved by about as much as the cellists did. The readers “never so much as held an instrument”, so their improvement did not come from playing.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches the result. A says the readers did not improve at all, B says they improved much more on every measure, and C gives them instrument practice that they never had.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The book-club readers improved by about as much as the cellists. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A comparison group is often expected to show no change, so a reader who expects the cellists to win may assume that the readers stood still.
distractors.why_wrong: The readers’ scores climbed by roughly the same margin as the cellists’ scores (step 2), so they did improve.

distractors.why_tempting: The readers’ result is the surprise of the text, and a surprise is easy to remember as a win for the readers.
distractors.why_wrong: “Roughly the same margin” means about equal, not considerably more, and the text reports no measure on which the readers did better (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Practice and music run through the whole text, so it is easy to imagine that the readers did some playing too.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that the readers “never so much as held an instrument” (step 3). Their weekly work was reading a difficult chapter and defending a reading of it.

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks what a comparison showed, find the sentence that sets the two groups side by side and check two things: the direction (better, worse or about the same) and the size of the difference.
p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not let the result you expect replace the result the text reports. Many readers expect the musicians to win, but the text reports about the same improvement in both groups.

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The cellists and the book-club readers improved by about as much, so the text looks for what the two activities shared: a fixed weekly commitment, other people expecting you to come, and hard work at getting better. B describes that routine. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the text does not state the cause outright, so you have to work it out from what it does say. The question is about both groups, so the cause must fit both the cellists and the readers.

steps.title: Start from the result
steps.text: The two groups improved by roughly the same margin, and the text concludes: “Whatever was lifting the numbers, it did not appear to be music as such.”

steps.title: Find what they shared
steps.text: The next sentence lists what the two activities had in common: “a fixed weekly commitment, a room full of other people expecting you to show, and the slow, faintly uncomfortable labor of getting better at something genuinely hard.” Regular, social and effortful – that is the routine in B.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names the shared routine. A credits the cello, which the readers never played; C names friendships, which the text never mentions, and makes them the whole cause of every gain; and D brings in a testing effect that the text never raises.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: What both groups shared was a regular, demanding routine done with other people. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Pellerham points to music’s “unusual demands on timing and memory”, and the cello is the focus of the study, so its special skills seem a natural cause.
distractors.why_wrong: Cello skills cannot explain why the book-club readers, who never played, improved by about as much (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does stress company – “a room full of other people expecting you to show” – so a social cause sounds right.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions friendships, and company is only one of the three things it lists, alongside the fixed weekly commitment and the hard work (step 3). C also says the friendships “fully accounted for every participant's gain”, which goes far beyond the text.

distractors.why_tempting: Scores can rise just because people get used to a test, and the volunteers were tested before and after the course, so D can sound like a sharp point about method.
distractors.why_wrong: The question asks what the text suggests, and the text never raises this possibility. The cause it points to is what the two activities had in common (step 3).

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “suggest” questions about a cause, look for what the text sets aside and what it puts in its place. Here it sets aside music and lists what the two activities shared; the right option restates that list.
p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not bring in a cause from outside the text, however reasonable it sounds. A testing effect may be real in general, but this text never mentions it.

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer calls the idea “an appealing thought” and grants that Pellerham “may well turn out to be right”, but says that the data “point somewhere more sober”. Appealing, but not where the evidence points – that is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to one claim: that music has a special power to “rejuvenate” the ageing brain, which means to make it young again. Keep the writer’s own voice apart from Pellerham’s.

steps.title: Find the claim
steps.text: The claim is voiced by Pellerham, whose hunch is that music “carries a power we simply haven’t learned to measure yet”. That is the enthusiast’s view, and the text reports it in Pellerham’s words.

steps.title: Find the writer’s verdict
steps.text: The writer answers: “It is an appealing thought, and Pellerham may well turn out to be right.” Then comes the turn: “For now, though, the Tessendale data, taken on their own terms, point somewhere more sober.” The writer grants the appeal but follows the evidence, which points to effort rather than music.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches: appealing, but the evidence points elsewhere. B makes the writer sure of something that even Pellerham calls only a hunch, C makes the writer look down on the idea, and D turns a polite concession – admitting that someone else could be right – into the writer’s own forecast.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer finds the idea appealing but thinks the evidence points elsewhere. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The most quotable sentence about music’s power comes from Pellerham, so it is easy to hand that view to the writer and make it firmer.
distractors.why_wrong: Even Pellerham calls the idea a “hunch”. The writer’s own verdict is that the data “point somewhere more sober” (step 3), so “sure” is far from the writer’s position.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer ends by saying that the instrument is optional, so a negative word can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer calls the idea “an appealing thought” and allows that Pellerham “may well turn out to be right” (step 3). That is polite caution, not mockery.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does say that Pellerham “may well turn out to be right”, which can sound like hope that music will prove special.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a concession, not a forecast. Right after it, the writer says that the data “point somewhere more sober” (step 3), and the text ends: “The instrument is optional. The effort is not.”

p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, find the writer’s own judgement and keep it apart from the people quoted. Then check both the direction and the strength: here the writer grants the idea some appeal but leans against it.
p5-elf-b1-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: A polite concession such as “may well turn out to be right” is not the same as sharing that view. Read the sentence that follows it – here “For now, though, …” – to find where the writer stands.

p5-elf-b1-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The owls begin hunting almost exactly eleven minutes after the bats leave their roosts, because the bats flush up the moths that the owls eat. When the bats were delayed, the owls were delayed too. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what prompts the owls to begin hunting – what sets their hunting off. “According to the text” means that the answer must be stated there.

steps.title: Find the timing
steps.text: Venn found that “the owls begin hunting almost precisely eleven minutes after the local bats leave their roosts each evening”. The next sentences explain why: “The bats, sweeping the air first, flush up dense clouds of night-flying moths, and the owls simply harvest the insects the bats shake loose.” To flush up is to drive up into the air.

steps.title: Check the test
steps.text: An experiment supports it: “When Venn's team delayed the bats' departure with dimmed artificial light, the owls' first strikes slipped later by the very same interval.” When the bats left later, the owls started later.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C names the bats’ departure and the moths it stirs up. A gives a cause that the text never mentions, B is ruled out by the experiment, and D says that the owls chase the bats, which the text denies.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The bats’ departure sets the owls’ hunt going. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A drop in temperature at nightfall sounds like a natural reason for insects to move, and the option mentions the ridgeline perches from the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions temperature. It says that the moths rise because the bats flush them up (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Owls hunt at dusk, so fading light sounds like an obvious signal.
distractors.why_wrong: The text explains the timing by the bats, which flush up the moths that the owls eat (step 2). And when the bats were held back, the owls started later by the same interval (step 3). A fixed internal clock would not have moved.

distractors.why_tempting: Owls are predators, and following the bats sounds like a clever way to find food.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “Crucially, the owls do not chase the bats through the trees; they wait at fixed perches along the ridgelines, letting the disturbed moths rise to meet them.”

p5-elf-b1-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a question asks what triggers something, look for the event the text ties it to in time, and for any test that changes that event. Here the bats leave, the owls start hunting almost exactly eleven minutes later, and delaying the bats delays the owls.
p5-elf-b1-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Options that sound like general knowledge about owls – dusk, temperature – are tempting, but the text names a different trigger. Answer from the text, not from what owls usually do.

p5-elf-b1-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: A ship that reached the quay safely paid the keepers a toll, and a ship that ran aground paid nothing. So the keepers earned money only when ships arrived safely, which gave them a strong reason to keep the lamps lit. D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the text does not state the reason outright. Find the facts it gives about the keepers and work out the one step that links them to the lamps that stayed lit.

steps.title: Find how the keepers were paid
steps.text: The keepers were paid “not by the town council but directly by the ships that used the harbour”, and “A vessel that reached the quay safely paid the keepers a fixed toll; a vessel that ran aground paid nothing at all.”

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: A wreck cost the keepers that ship’s toll, so a dark lantern hurt them directly. Keeping the lamps lit was in their own interest. The comparison in the text fits this: when the neighbouring town paid its keepers a salary from taxes, its wreck rate climbed within a decade.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D draws exactly this link. A puts the council in charge of the keepers, B brings in Baltic ports in general, and C treats the toll as a steady income, which leaves out the condition attached to it.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The keepers were paid only for safe arrivals, so keeping the lamps lit paid off for them. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: The text mentions the council’s records and discipline, so the council can seem to be the force behind the keepers.
distractors.why_wrong: The keepers were paid “not by the town council” (step 2), and the records show only that the council never once had to discipline a keeper for a darkened lantern. Nothing says that it watched the guild closely.

distractors.why_tempting: Strict guild rules are a familiar idea from history, and Vellmar was a Baltic port.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says nothing about Baltic ports in general. Its own comparison is with a neighbouring town whose wreck rate rose after it changed how its keepers were paid, which points to the pay, not the region (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: C uses the text’s own words – “a fixed toll” – and a steady income sounds like a good reason to work well.
distractors.why_wrong: Not every ship paid: a ship that ran aground “paid nothing at all” (step 2). The pay depended on a safe arrival, and that condition is what links the pay to the lamps. The neighbouring town’s keepers had a salary, and its wreck rate rose.

p5-elf-b1-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “suggest … why” questions, list the facts the text gives and look for the one-step link between them. Here the pay rule and the lamps that stayed lit are both stated; the right answer supplies the link – the keepers’ own interest.
p5-elf-b1-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not stop at an option that repeats a phrase from the text. C quotes “a fixed toll” but drops the condition attached to it, and the condition is the whole point.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text reports a trial of fog nets on two slopes of one ridge. They helped seedlings survive where the fog was thick and made almost no difference where it was thin, and the writer concludes that the nets “earn their keep where the fog is already thick and dependable”. C sums this up. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text. The right answer must cover the trial’s mixed result and the conclusion the writer draws from it.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph presents fog nets as an old, appealing idea and narrows the question to whether they keep young trees alive. The second reports a clear gain on the foggy seaward slope, the third almost no effect on the hazy leeward slope, the fourth an engineer’s bold claims, and the fifth the writer’s verdict.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The last paragraph says: “The nets earn their keep where the fog is already thick and dependable”, and “Where the fog runs thin, the screens have little to catch”. To earn your keep is to be worth what you cost, and “dependable” means reliable, the word C uses.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C states the verdict. A turns the engineer’s pitch into the conclusion, B reports a breakthrough in mesh design that the text never mentions, and D makes a claim about native trees that the text never makes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about where fog nets work: where the fog is reliable. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The text calls the idea “old, cheap, and almost impossibly appealing”, and Kessler claims that the nets can green any dry shore the fog reaches.
distractors.why_wrong: On the leeward slope the nets “bought almost nothing”, so the trial does not show that they work almost anywhere. The writer calls Kessler’s view “a stirring pitch” and draws a far smaller conclusion (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text is about mesh and water from fog, and B uses that vocabulary.
distractors.why_wrong: The text reports no new design. The panels were “nothing exotic”, ordinary greenhouse netting, and the trial was about keeping seedlings alive, not about cost at scale.

distractors.why_tempting: The seedlings were native thorn trees, and the first paragraph mentions “the deserts that keep spreading”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never compares tree planting with other ways of fighting deserts. Its subject is whether the nets help planted seedlings survive (step 2).

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions, check that the option covers the turn in the text as well as the opening. Here the text starts with a big promise and ends with a narrower verdict; the right answer is the verdict.
p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: The most confident claim in a text is not always its main point. Kessler’s pitch is the boldest sentence, but the writer goes on to answer it.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The second paragraph says that after two dry seasons most of the netted seedlings on the seaward slope were still alive, “on the order of two in three”. About two-thirds – that is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about one group: the netted seedlings on the seaward slope. Keep them apart from the unnetted seedlings and from the leeward slope.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “After two dry seasons, most of the netted seedlings there were still alive, on the order of two in three, while barely a fifth of the unnetted plants had survived.” “There” is the seaward slope, “the flank that meets the morning fog head-on”.

steps.title: Match the numbers
steps.text: “On the order of two in three” means about two-thirds, so A keeps both the figure and the time frame of two dry seasons.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches. B turns “most” into every seedling, C describes the leeward slope, and D compares growth with the hand-watered seedlings, which the text never does.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: About two-thirds of the netted seedlings on the seaward slope survived two dry seasons. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The seaward result was a clear success, so it is easy to remember it as complete.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says “most”, about two in three, not all (step 2). B turns a strong result into a perfect one.

distractors.why_tempting: C is true of the leeward slope, where the netted and unnetted seedlings died at much the same rate.
distractors.why_wrong: The question is about the seaward slope. There the netted seedlings did far better: about two in three survived, against barely a fifth of the unnetted plants (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does mention a hand-watered group, so a comparison with it can seem to belong here.
distractors.why_wrong: The hand-watered seedlings were on the leeward slope, and the text reports how many seedlings survived, not how fast any of them grew.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a text gives results for several groups, note which group the question names and find the sentences about that group. Wrong options often borrow a result from a neighbouring group.
p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Two slopes, netted and unnetted seedlings and a hand-watered group give several results that are easy to mix up. Tie each figure to its group before you compare.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: On the leeward slope the nets “bought almost nothing”, but a small hand-watered group did well: roughly seven in ten survived. B gives both halves. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what happened on the leeward slope, the side behind the crest of the ridge. That slope is described in the third paragraph.

steps.title: Find the result for the nets
steps.text: “On the leeward slope, tucked behind the crest where the fog thins to a haze, the panels bought almost nothing: the netted and unnetted seedlings died at much the same rate”.

steps.title: Find what did work
steps.text: “A small group on that same dry ground had been watered by hand, a few liters a week hauled in by truck, and roughly seven in ten of them pulled through”. “Pulled through” means survived.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B combines the two results. A says that no seedling survived, C reverses the comparison between the slopes, and D says that the hand-watering was stopped, which the text never says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The nets made little difference on the leeward slope, while most of the hand-watered seedlings survived. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The nets failed on the leeward slope, so it can seem that nothing survived there.
distractors.why_wrong: The nets “bought almost nothing”, which is not the same as nothing, and roughly seven in ten of the hand-watered seedlings on that slope survived (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: C mentions both slopes, as the text does, so it looks like a fair comparison.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the other way round: the nets helped on the seaward slope and “bought almost nothing” on the leeward one (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text says that the water truck broke an axle twice, which can suggest that hand-watering was too much trouble.
distractors.why_wrong: The broken axle shows how harsh the ground is, but the text never says that the watering stopped or what it cost. It reports that the hand-watered seedlings did well (step 3).

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks what happened in one place, read the whole account of that place. Here the nets’ result and the hand-watered group are in the same paragraph, and the right answer needs both.
p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Watch for absolute words that go beyond the text. “Almost nothing” is not “nothing”, and a failure of the nets is not a failure of every seedling.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Where the fog was thin, the nets bought almost nothing, and the writer adds that where the fog runs thin, “the screens have little to catch”. On a coast with only occasional fog, the nets would likely help little. That is D. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Imply” means that the answer is not stated directly. The text never discusses such a coast, so apply what the trial showed to it.

steps.title: Find the closest case in the trial
steps.text: The leeward slope is the trial’s fog-poor case: there the fog “thins to a haze”, and the panels “bought almost nothing”.

steps.title: Add the writer’s verdict
steps.text: The last paragraph says: “Where the fog runs thin, the screens have little to catch, and no width of mesh can conjure moisture from a dry sky.” To conjure something is to make it appear as if by magic.

steps.title: Apply it to occasional fog
steps.text: The nets earn their keep where the fog is “thick and dependable”, and what seemed to help the seedlings was “water, arriving often enough to matter”. Occasional fog is not dependable, so a coast with only occasional fog is in the same position as the hazy slope.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D follows by one step. A carries the seaward slope’s figure over to a coast without much fog, B builds on Kessler’s claim, which the trial does not support, and C says that the trees need almost no water, which the trial contradicts.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: With little fog to catch, the nets would probably help little. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Two in three is the most memorable figure in the text, and it is a real result for netted seedlings.
distractors.why_wrong: That figure comes from the seaward slope, which meets the fog head-on. On the fog-poor leeward slope the nets made almost no difference (step 2), so the figure cannot be carried over to a coast with little fog.

distractors.why_tempting: Kessler says that “the fog reaches a great deal more of the world than anyone has bothered to measure”, so B sounds like something the text reports.
distractors.why_wrong: B builds on Kessler’s claim and stretches it: Kessler says the fog reaches “a great deal more of the world than anyone has bothered to measure”, not almost everywhere. And fog reaching a coast is not enough: the leeward slope got fog too, as a thin haze, and the nets “bought almost nothing” there (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Thorn trees sound tough, and desert plants are often thought to need little water.
distractors.why_wrong: The trial shows the opposite. On the seaward slope “barely a fifth of the unnetted plants had survived”, and on the leeward slope the hand-watered group did “better than anything the nets had managed on the fog-poor slope”. The seedlings needed water.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “imply” questions about a new situation, find the case in the text that is most like it and carry over that result, no further. Here a coast with occasional fog is most like the hazy leeward slope.
p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not carry a number over from the wrong case. The two-in-three survival belongs to the fog-rich slope, so it says nothing about a coast where fog is rare.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer calls Kessler’s view “a stirring pitch” and grants that Kessler “may yet be proved partly right”, but says that the trial “points somewhere more modest than the pitch”: the nets work where the fog is already thick and dependable. Drawn to the promise, doubtful beyond fog-rich sites – that is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to the idea that the nets could green dry coasts in general. Keep the writer’s voice apart from Kessler’s.

steps.title: Find the idea
steps.text: The writer introduces the idea in the first paragraph as “old, cheap, and almost impossibly appealing”. Kessler states it most boldly: “We can green any dry shore the fog reaches”.

steps.title: Find the writer’s verdict
steps.text: The writer answers: “It is a stirring pitch, and Kessler may yet be proved partly right; the seaward plots are, after all, real, and they are still standing.” A stirring pitch is an exciting sales message. Then: “For now, though, the Corvane trial points somewhere more modest than the pitch.” The nets earn their keep where the fog is already thick and dependable.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches: drawn to the promise but doubtful beyond foggy sites. B gives the writer Kessler’s confidence, C turns the writer’s reserve into contempt, and D overlooks the writer’s clear verdict.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer is cautious: the nets work where the fog is thick and dependable, but for now the writer doubts the broader promise. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The text quotes Kessler’s confident claim at length, and that confidence is easy to hand to the writer.
distractors.why_wrong: The confidence is Kessler’s. The writer says that the trial “points somewhere more modest than the pitch” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer ends by calling the smaller promise perhaps “the only honest one”, which can sound like a rejection of the whole idea.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer grants that “the seaward plots are, after all, real” and that the nets “earn their keep” where the fog is thick and dependable (step 3). That is cautious support for a limited use, not contempt for a gimmick.

distractors.why_tempting: Most of the text reports the trial, so the writer can seem to stay neutral.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer gives a clear view: the trial “points somewhere more modest than the pitch” (step 3), and the smaller promise may also be “the only honest one”.

p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, find where the writer speaks in their own voice, often just after a quoted person. Words such as “For now, though” often mark the turn from a concession to the writer’s real verdict.
p5-elf-b2-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: A concession such as “may yet be proved partly right” is not agreement. The writer’s verdict comes after it.

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The sentences after the gap describe the response: rivals assumed the scheme was a stunt, and some were blunter still. That is mockery, and the word for mockery is “derision”. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the response from the rest of the industry was one of near-universal ___”. It names how other firms reacted to Aldermere’s four-day week.

steps.title: Read on for the reaction
steps.text: The next sentences describe it: “Competitors assumed the scheme was a recruitment stunt”, and “A few were blunter still.” Dismissing a plan as a stunt is scornful, so the gap needs a word for scorn or mockery: “derision”.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: All four options end in -ision. “Revision” means a change, “provision” means a supply or an arrangement, and “precision” means exactness. None of them is a scornful reaction.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Near-universal derision” – mockery from almost everyone – is the only fit. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: A new scheme might lead other firms to rethink their own plans, and “revision” means a change of that kind.
distractors.why_wrong: The next sentences show scorn, not rethinking: rivals assumed the scheme was “a recruitment stunt” (step 2). The text never says that other firms changed their plans.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence is about working conditions, and “provision” is a common word in that kind of text.
distractors.why_wrong: A provision is a supply or an arrangement, not a reaction. “One of near-universal provision” makes no sense as a response (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: “Precision” is a familiar word with the same -ision ending as the other options, and it sounds formal enough for a business text.
distractors.why_wrong: Precision means exactness. The rivals did not react with exactness; they reacted with mockery (step 2).

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap names a reaction, read the next sentences: they usually describe the reaction in more detail. Here “stunt” and “blunter still” point to mockery.
p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: The four options look almost the same because they share the -ision ending. Choose by meaning, not by look.

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The critics predicted trouble: once the charm of three-day weekends had faded and the same work had to be squeezed into fewer hours, output would fall sharply – it would slump. The next paragraph confirms that a fall was the fear: output “did not fall at all”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “They predicted that output would ___ within a single quarter”. “They” are the blunter critics, so the prediction is a warning.

steps.title: Follow the reason
steps.text: The critics give a reason: “once the charm of three-day weekends had faded and the same volume of work had to be forced into fewer hours”. In their view, squeezing the same work into fewer hours would make output drop.

steps.title: Check the answer to the prediction
steps.text: The next paragraph replies: “output per employee did not fall at all”. That confirms that the critics had predicted a fall. “Slump” means a sudden, steep fall, and it is a common verb for output, sales or prices.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Output would slump within a single quarter” is the critics’ warning. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “Surge” is a strong verb often used about output, and it fits the grammar.
distractors.why_wrong: A surge is a sudden rise. Critics who saw the scheme as a stunt were not predicting a rise, and the next paragraph treats their forecast as a fall that never came (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Output did in fact hold steady and edge upward, so “stabilise” matches what happened.
distractors.why_wrong: The gap holds the critics’ prediction, not the result. They warned of a fall, and stabilising is not a warning (steps 2–3).

distractors.why_tempting: “Wither” also means to decline, so it points in the right direction.
distractors.why_wrong: “Wither” describes a slow drying up, as with plants or hopes, and it is not the usual verb for output. The critics expected a quick, sharp fall “within a single quarter”, and that is a slump (step 3).

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a gap holds a prediction, work out what the people predicting expect. Then check the text’s answer to the prediction: here “did not fall at all” shows that a fall was predicted.
p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Do not fill the gap with what actually happened. The sentence reports the critics’ forecast, and the forecast was wrong.

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The sentence before the gap says that the result was not an unqualified success, and the gapped sentence gives evidence for that: the gains were concentrated in two of the firm’s seven departments. A connective that confirms and strengthens a point is “Indeed”. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, the gains were concentrated in two of the firm's seven departments”. The sentence before it says: “The result was not, for all that, an unqualified success.” An unqualified success is a complete one, with no reservations.

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The gapped sentence does not contrast with the one before; it supports it. Gains concentrated in two departments show why the success was not complete, so the connective must confirm the point.

steps.title: Check the connectives
steps.text: “Indeed” adds evidence for what was just said. “However” and “Conversely” signal a contrast or an opposite, and “Otherwise” means “if not” or “in other respects”. None of those fits a sentence that supports the one before.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Indeed, the gains were concentrated in two of the firm's seven departments” supports the claim before it. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph turns from good news to limits, and “However” is the usual word for a turn.
distractors.why_wrong: The turn has already been made in the sentence before: “The result was not, for all that, an unqualified success.” The gapped sentence continues that point instead of turning against it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Otherwise” is a common linking word and can seem to introduce another side of the result.
distractors.why_wrong: “Otherwise” means “if not” or “in other respects”, and neither meaning links these sentences. The gapped sentence gives evidence for the one before it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Conversely” sounds formal and analytical, which suits a report on figures.
distractors.why_wrong: “Conversely” introduces the opposite of what came before. The gapped sentence says the same thing as the one before – the success had limits – so there is no opposite (step 2).

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: For a connective gap, decide how the gapped sentence relates to the one before it: does it add evidence, contrast, give a result or mark time? Here it adds evidence, which is the job of “Indeed”.
p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: A sentence about problems after good news can make “However” feel automatic. Check what comes directly before the gap: here the contrast has already been made, and the gapped sentence backs it up.

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Aldous is cautious about the firm’s own result and warns that, without its settled clients, the year might have looked very different. “Reticent” means reserved or holding back, and here Aldous holds back from claiming more than the numbers show. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “She remains notably ___ about how far the numbers can be stretched.” To stretch the numbers is to claim more than they show.

steps.title: Use what follows
steps.text: Aldous adds a warning: “Take away our unusually settled list of clients” – “and the same year might have read very differently.” The verb “cautions” and the sentence before, where Aldous “is the first to say so”, show someone holding back from big claims, and the next paragraph names the attitude: “That restraint is worth heeding.” “Reticent” means reserved or holding back.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Insistent” means firmly pressing a point, the opposite of holding back. “Consistent” means unchanging or in agreement, and “prevalent” means widespread, which describes how common something is, not a person.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Notably reticent about how far the numbers can be stretched” describes Aldous’s caution. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Founders often defend their own schemes firmly, so a word for pressing a point can seem likely.
distractors.why_wrong: “Insistent” means firmly pushing a claim. With the firm’s own numbers Aldous does the opposite: the warning that the year “might have read very differently” holds back, and the next paragraph calls this “restraint” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Aldous “is the first to say so”, and “consistent” can sound like a fair word for someone who keeps telling the same honest story.
distractors.why_wrong: “Consistent” says nothing about holding back, but the warning that follows and the word “restraint” in the next paragraph show that the gap needs a word for caution (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Prevalent” is a formal word that looks at home in a report on figures.
distractors.why_wrong: “Prevalent” means widespread, as with a disease or a habit. It tells you how common something is, so it cannot describe how one person behaves (step 3).

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a gap describes a person’s attitude, look for what the person says next. Here the warning “might have read very differently” shows caution, so the gap needs a word for holding back.
p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: “Insistent” and “reticent” are opposites. If you read only “She remains notably ___”, either could fit; the quotation after the gap decides.

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The paragraph asks whether a scheme that worked in one comfortable software firm would work elsewhere, such as in a factory or a hospital. A result that can be carried over to other settings is “transferable”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Whether an arrangement that flatters a small, loyal, comfortably financed software house is genuinely ___ to a factory floor or a hospital ward”. Here “flatters” means makes look good.

steps.title: Follow the argument
steps.text: The sentence before says that the conditions behind Aldermere’s success – “deep reserves, patient clients, a young and portable workforce” – are “precisely the ones that most firms lack”. So the question is whether the scheme can be carried over to very different workplaces.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: All four options can be followed by “to”, so grammar does not decide. “Answerable to” means accountable to someone, “agreeable to” means acceptable to someone, and “amenable to” means open to something, as in “amenable to change”. Only “transferable to” means able to be carried over to another setting.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Genuinely transferable to a factory floor or a hospital ward” completes the argument. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “Answerable to” is a common phrase, and the sentence is about whether the arrangement holds up.
distractors.why_wrong: “Answerable to” means accountable to a person or a body, such as a manager. A scheme is not accountable to a factory floor (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: “Agreeable” suggests that workers in a factory or a hospital might like the scheme, which sounds relevant.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph is not about whether people would like the scheme but about whether it can be carried over to workplaces that lack the conditions that made it work (step 2). “Agreeable to a factory floor” is not a natural way to say that.

distractors.why_tempting: “Amenable to” is also followed by “to” and means open to something, which can sound close to the right meaning.
distractors.why_wrong: A workplace might be amenable to a scheme, but a scheme is not amenable to a workplace. The question the paragraph raises is whether the scheme can be carried over, and that is what “transferable” means (step 2).

p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When all the options take the same word after them – here “to” – grammar cannot decide. Work out what the sentence asks, then choose the word with that meaning.
p5-elf-b2-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Words that end in -able look alike. Check what each one means with “to”: transferable to a setting, answerable to a person, agreeable to someone, amenable to an idea.

p5-elf-b2-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: A spreading crack tears open the tiny clay capsules, and the slurry inside seeps into the gap and hardens. Reyes stresses that the trigger is “the cracking itself”. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what makes the additive seal a crack – what starts the repair. “According to the text” means that the answer is stated there.

steps.title: Find the mechanism
steps.text: “When a hairline crack spreads through the concrete and tears open a capsule, the slurry seeps into the gap, reacts with moisture in the surrounding air, and hardens into calcite, knitting the crack shut.”

steps.title: Find the trigger
steps.text: The next sentence names it outright: “The trigger, Reyes stresses, is the cracking itself — not a rise in temperature, and not any chemical brushed on afterward.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names the crack and what it does to the capsules. A and C are the two causes that the text rules out, and D gives moisture a job that the text does not give it.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The crack itself sets off the repair. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Heat often speeds up chemical reactions, so temperature sounds like a likely trigger.
distractors.why_wrong: The text rules it out: the trigger is “not a rise in temperature” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Brushing a sealant onto a crack is a familiar way to repair concrete.
distractors.why_wrong: The text rules this out too: the trigger is “not any chemical brushed on afterward” (step 3). The point of the additive is that the concrete repairs itself.

distractors.why_tempting: Moisture in the air is part of the process, so it looks like a fair answer.
distractors.why_wrong: Moisture plays a different part: the freed slurry “reacts with moisture in the surrounding air” and hardens (step 2). Moisture does not dissolve the capsules, and the text names the crack, not the moisture, as the trigger.

p5-elf-b2-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text names a cause and then rules out others, the ruled-out causes often become wrong options. Mark the “not … not …” list and cross those options off.
p5-elf-b2-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: D uses a real part of the process – moisture – but gives it the wrong job. Check what the text says each part does, not just whether it is mentioned.

p5-elf-b2-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The fair disappears from the ledgers after 1631, and the next Michaelmas pages go entirely to a river wall that cost more than the fair had ever earned and was built on the meadow where the stalls had stood. The clues suggest that the wall took both the money and the ground, so the fair lapsed. That is D. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the answer is not stated directly: the text never says why the fair disappeared. Collect the clues it gives and find the explanation they point to.

steps.title: Note the silence
steps.text: After the autumn of 1631 the fair “vanishes from the ledgers altogether”, and “No line records its cancellation”, although the same careful chamberlain “noted even the cost of mending a single lock”.

steps.title: Find what replaced it
steps.text: “The pages for the following Michaelmas are given over entirely to work on the river wall, which that season devoured a sum far larger than the fair had ever yielded — and which was raised, the entries show, on the very meadow where the stalls had once stood.”

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: The wall swallowed the town’s money and was built on the fair’s own ground. The clues point to one explanation: the works took over both, and the fair quietly came to an end. That is what “lapsed” means in D: it ended without any formal decision.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D draws that link. A says the fair went on as before, although the river wall was built on its meadow; B brings in a trend across England that the text never mentions; and C invents a formal order that the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The river wall seems to have taken both the town’s money and the fair’s meadow, so the fair lapsed. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A fair could in principle carry on without being recorded, and the text stresses the silence in the books.
distractors.why_wrong: The chamberlain recorded even the cost of mending a lock (step 2), and the river wall was built on the very meadow where the stalls had stood (step 3). A fair that “carried on as before” does not fit either fact.

distractors.why_tempting: A wider trend is a familiar kind of explanation in history.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says nothing about fairs elsewhere in England. All its clues are local: the ledgers, the river wall and the meadow (steps 2–3).

distractors.why_tempting: Fairs were sometimes ended by an official order, and a missing record might hide one.
distractors.why_wrong: The text mentions no order at all. C has to invent one and then assume that a chamberlain who “noted even the cost of mending a single lock” chose to leave it out. The river wall explains the end of the fair with what the ledgers do show (step 3).

p5-elf-b2-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “suggest … why” questions about an event the text never explains, list the clues it does give and pick the option that links them in one step. Here the money and the meadow both point to the river wall.
p5-elf-b2-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not fill a silence in the record with something the text never mentions, such as an unrecorded order or a national trend. Use the clues the record does give: here the money and the meadow.

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Operators thought that a traveller in a hurry would always fly, so one after another they stopped running their night trains. The usual verb for taking a service out of use is “withdraw”: “withdrew its overnight services”. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “One national operator after another quietly ___ its overnight services”. The reason follows: the operators thought that “a traveller in a hurry would always take the early flight”.

steps.title: Find the verb that goes with “services”
steps.text: The sleeper train “looked like a relic”, and one operator after another was ending its night trains. A company that stops offering a service withdraws it, so “withdrew its overnight services” is the natural choice here.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: “Dismissed” is used for people, ideas or fears; “declined” with an object means refused, as in declining an offer; and “renounced” means formally gave up a right, a title or a belief. None of them is used for taking a train service off the timetable.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Quietly withdrew its overnight services” is the only natural completion. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The sleeper train “looked like a relic”, and to dismiss something can mean to reject it as old-fashioned or unimportant.
distractors.why_wrong: You can dismiss an idea or an employee, but an operator does not dismiss its own services. The sentence describes trains being taken out of service, and the verb for that is “withdrew” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The number of sleeper trains did decline, so the word fits the story.
distractors.why_wrong: In that sense “decline” takes no object: services decline, but an operator does not decline its services. With an object, “decline” means to refuse, as in declining an invitation (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: To renounce is to give something up, and the operators did give up their night trains.
distractors.why_wrong: “Renounce” is used for giving up a right, a title or a belief, usually in a formal statement. Stopping a train service is not renouncing it; the usual verb is “withdraw” (step 2).

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: In a verb gap, look at the object – here “its overnight services” – and ask which verb normally goes with it. Several of these verbs mean reject or give up, but only one of them is used for ending a service.
p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: “Declined” is tempting because sleeper trains did decline. But with an object it means refused, so read the whole frame, not just the verb.

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The longer routes lost money, and no ministry seemed willing to keep covering those losses for ever. To promise to pay for a loss is to “underwrite” it. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the longer routes ran at a loss that no transport ministry seemed willing to ___ indefinitely”. A ministry pays for transport, so the question is whether it would keep paying for the loss.

steps.title: Find the verb
steps.text: To underwrite a loss is to promise to cover it with money. “Willing to underwrite” the loss “indefinitely” means willing to keep paying for it with no end date.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: “Condone” means to accept bad behaviour, “overturn” means to reverse a decision, and “dispel” means to drive away doubts or fears. A financial loss is none of these things.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The frame now reads “a loss that no transport ministry seemed willing to underwrite indefinitely”: no ministry seemed willing to keep paying for the loss. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Losses can sound like something a ministry might put up with, and “condone” means to accept or put up with something bad.
distractors.why_wrong: “Condone” is used for behaviour that is wrong, as in condoning cheating. A loss is not wrongdoing, so a ministry does not condone it (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Ministries do overturn decisions, so the word fits the world of government.
distractors.why_wrong: You overturn a decision or a ruling. A ministry does not overturn a loss that keeps running; the sentence is about paying for it (step 1).

distractors.why_tempting: Ministries try to dispel worries, and the routes were a cause for worry.
distractors.why_wrong: “Dispel” takes doubts, fears or myths as its object. A loss is a sum of money that someone has to pay, not a fear to drive away (step 2).

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When the object of the verb is money – here “a loss” – look for the verb that is used with money. Words that fit the setting can still be wrong for the object.
p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Each wrong verb can sound official: condoning, overturning, dispelling. But none of them means paying for “a loss”.

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The planners expected to fill perhaps half the cabins on a good night, but the first season sold out weeks in advance. The result was the opposite of what they expected, and “Instead” marks exactly that. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens “___, the first season sold out weeks in advance”. Just before it: “its planners expected to fill perhaps half the cabins on a good night”.

steps.title: Compare the two sentences
steps.text: The planners expected to fill perhaps half the cabins on a good night; the first season sold out. The gapped sentence reports what happened in place of what was expected, so the connective must mark a result against expectation.

steps.title: Check the connectives
steps.text: “Instead” means in place of what was expected. “Accordingly” means as a result, in line with what came before; “Otherwise” means if not, or in other respects; and “Meanwhile” means at the same time. Only “Instead” marks the reversal.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Instead, the first season sold out weeks in advance” is the only natural reading. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Accordingly” is a formal linking word, and the second sentence does follow the first in time.
distractors.why_wrong: “Accordingly” means that what follows is in line with what came before. Selling out does not follow from expecting to fill perhaps half the cabins on a good night; it defeats that expectation (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Otherwise” can introduce something different, and the result was different from the plan.
distractors.why_wrong: “Otherwise” means “if not” or “in other respects”. Neither meaning fits: the sentence reports what actually happened in place of the expected result (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The relaunch and the first season happened in the same period, so a time word can seem natural.
distractors.why_wrong: “Meanwhile” introduces a second thing happening at the same time. The sold-out season is not a separate event beside the planners’ expectation; it is what happened instead (step 2).

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: For a connective gap, compare what the sentence before expects with what the gapped sentence reports. When the result defeats the expectation, look for a word such as “Instead” or “But”.
p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: “Accordingly” looks formal and clever, but it means the opposite of what is needed here: it signals a result that goes along with what came before.

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Yet” turns from the success story to its weak points: almost all the new lines survive on public money, and their carriages are old and costly to run. The revival is less secure than the headlines suggest – more “precarious”. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Yet the revival is a good deal more ___ than the cheering headlines suggest.” “Yet” signals a turn against the good news of the paragraph before.

steps.title: Use the evidence
steps.text: Verholt points out that almost all the new lines “survive on public subsidy” and that the carriages are “decades old and costly to keep running”. A revival that depends on subsidy and ageing trains is at risk. That is what “precarious” means: unstable and likely to fail.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Auspicious” means promising a good future, “gregarious” means fond of company, and “meticulous” means very careful. None of them describes a revival that rests on subsidy.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “A good deal more precarious than the cheering headlines suggest” fits the turn and the evidence. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The night train came back into fashion, and one relaunched service sold out its first season, so a positive word seems to suit the revival.
distractors.why_wrong: “Yet” turns against the good news, and the evidence after the gap is about weakness: subsidy and old, costly carriages (step 2). “Auspicious” points the wrong way.

distractors.why_tempting: “Gregarious” sounds lively and positive, like the revival story in the paragraph before.
distractors.why_wrong: “Gregarious” describes people or animals who like company. A revival cannot be gregarious, and the sentence is about how secure the revival is (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Verholt has audited three of the new lines, and an audit is careful work, so a word for careful work can seem relevant.
distractors.why_wrong: “Meticulous” describes careful people or careful work. The sentence describes the revival, not the audit, and the evidence shows that the revival is at risk (step 2).

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: After a turn word such as “Yet”, expect the opposite of what came before. Then use the evidence that follows to choose between words of the right kind.
p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not let the cheerful paragraph before the gap choose the word. “Than the cheering headlines suggest” tells you that the gap says something less cheerful.

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Verholt warns that without the grants and the nostalgia, the accounts would look much worse. The idiom for a hopeful, favourable picture is “rosy”: the ledgers would look “far less rosy”. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits at the end of Verholt’s warning: “Take away the grants and the nostalgia” … “and the ledgers look far less ___.” Ledgers are account books, so the sentence is about how good the finances look.

steps.title: Find the idiom
steps.text: Without the grants and the nostalgia, the finances would look much worse. English says that a situation “looks rosy” when it looks hopeful and good, so “far less rosy” means much less favourable. That fits the warning.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Hollow” is used for promises or victories that mean nothing, “candid” means honest and open, and “generous” describes people who give a lot, or large amounts, as in a generous portion. None of them is a normal way to describe how accounts look.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The ledgers look far less rosy” – the finances look far worse. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Hollow” suggests emptiness, and the warning is that the finances are weak.
distractors.why_wrong: With “far less”, the word must name something good that the ledgers would lose. “Far less hollow” would mean that the finances look sounder, the opposite of the warning (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Account books should be honest, and “candid” means honest.
distractors.why_wrong: “Candid” describes people who speak openly. The warning is about how good the finances look, not about whether the books are honest (step 1).

distractors.why_tempting: Almost all the lines depend on grants, which are a kind of generous support.
distractors.why_wrong: “Generous” describes people who give a lot, or large portions. It is not the usual word for how accounts look; when finances look good, English says that they look “rosy” (step 2).

p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When a gap follows “far less” or “far more”, decide what quality is being reduced or increased. Here the ledgers look much worse, so the gap needs a word for a favourable picture.
p5-elf-b3-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: “Hollow” sounds negative, which matches the warning, but after “far less” it flips: less hollow means sounder. Check how the word works with the words around it.

p5-elf-b3-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: When the ice shifts, it stretches the frozen-in cable very slightly and changes the light scattered inside it. Reading those changes, the team can fix the position of each tiny fracture as the glacier moves. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the cable allows Ostrander’s team to do. Look for what the text says the team can do with it, and for what it says the method cannot do.

steps.title: Find how it works
steps.text: “A laser pulse sent down the fiber scatters faintly off flaws in the glass; when the surrounding ice shifts, it stretches the cable by a few billionths of a meter and alters that scattered light.”

steps.title: Find what it allows
steps.text: “Reading those changes, the team can fix the position of each tiny fracture as the glacier grinds downhill”. To fix the position of something is to locate it.

steps.title: Note the limit
steps.text: Ostrander adds that the method “shows only where the ice is cracking, not how much water is pooling beneath it”, and that for the water “the boreholes still have to be drilled and sampled by hand”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches: locating fractures by sensing tiny stretches. A is the thing the method cannot do, C contradicts what Ostrander says about the boreholes, and D misdescribes the laser.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The cable lets the team locate where the ice is cracking. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Meltwater is mentioned, and measuring water under a glacier sounds like the kind of thing such a tool would do.
distractors.why_wrong: Ostrander says that the method shows “only where the ice is cracking, not how much water is pooling beneath it” (step 4). Measuring meltwater is exactly what the cable cannot do.

distractors.why_tempting: A cable “doing the work of a thousand seismometers” sounds as if it could replace other methods.
distractors.why_wrong: Ostrander says that for the water “the boreholes still have to be drilled and sampled by hand” (step 4). The cable does not do away with them.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does describe a laser pulse sent down the fiber, so D uses real details.
distractors.why_wrong: The pulse “scatters faintly off flaws in the glass” (step 2); nothing in the text says that it melts ice. The laser is a way of reading the cable, not a source of heat.

p5-elf-b3-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text describes a tool, note both what it can do and what the text says it cannot do. Wrong options often take the limit and present it as a use.
p5-elf-b3-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Real details from the text can be put together in a wrong way. D keeps the laser and the ice but invents what the laser does to the ice.

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: A coat that is mended and passed on can return more value, across its owners, than one bought new and soon binned. Money and goods that keep moving from hand to hand are “in circulation”, so mending is the step that “keeps the value in circulation”. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the mending is not a sentimental flourish but the very step that keeps the value in ___”. The sentence explains the idea first: a coat “mended twice and passed on can return more, across its several owners, than one bought new and soon binned”.

steps.title: Find the fixed phrase
steps.text: The value moves from owner to owner. English uses “in circulation” for money or goods that keep passing from hand to hand, so “keeps the value in circulation” is the natural phrase.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: “In rotation” means taking turns, as with crops or staff; “in suspension” means held still or floating in a liquid; and “distribution” is used for goods being delivered, not for value that stays in use.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Mending keeps the value moving from owner to owner. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A coat that passes from owner to owner can seem to go round, which suggests rotation.
distractors.why_wrong: “In rotation” means taking turns in a fixed order, as with crops or staff. The idea here is value that keeps moving through many hands, and the phrase for that is “in circulation” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Suspension” is a formal word that sounds suitable for a sentence about value.
distractors.why_wrong: Something in suspension is held still or paused. The sentence says the opposite: mending keeps the value moving and in use (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Distribution” is an economic word, and the text is about trade in second-hand goods.
distractors.why_wrong: Goods can be in distribution while they are being delivered, but value is not kept in distribution. The phrase for value that stays in use is “in circulation” (step 2).

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap follows “keeps … in”, think of fixed phrases such as “in use” or “in circulation”. Then choose the one that matches what the sentence describes.
p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Several options are economic or formal words, which makes them sound right in a text about money. Test each one in the full phrase “keeps the value in ___”.

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: A repair bill is a cost, and few small workshops can pay it on their own. Taking a cost on yourself is “absorbing” it: “a repair bill that few can absorb alone”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Small workshops, though, face a repair bill that few can ___ alone”. The object of the verb is “a repair bill”, so the verb must describe what you do with a cost.

steps.title: Find the verb
steps.text: In business English, a firm absorbs a cost when it pays for it itself instead of passing it on. Few workshops can do that alone, and so volunteer cafés “have spread from town to town”.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: “Cushion” means to soften a blow or its effect, “alleviate” means to ease pain or hardship, and “dampen” means to reduce spirits or demand. Each one softens something, but none means paying a bill yourself.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “A repair bill that few can absorb alone” is the natural completion. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: A large bill is a blow to a small business, and “cushion” is used for softening a blow.
distractors.why_wrong: To cushion something is to soften its effect, often for someone else. The sentence asks whether a workshop can carry the whole bill itself, and the verb for taking on a cost is “absorb” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A repair bill is a burden, and “alleviate” is used for easing burdens.
distractors.why_wrong: You alleviate pain, poverty or pressure: you make a hard situation easier to bear. You do not alleviate a bill. The sentence asks who can pay it, and the verb for paying a cost yourself is “absorb” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Dampen” means to make something weaker, and the bill weakens the workshops.
distractors.why_wrong: You dampen spirits, enthusiasm or demand. The sentence is about who pays the bill, not about making it weaker (step 2).

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: In a verb gap, find the object – here “a repair bill” – and ask what we normally do with it. Costs are paid, covered or absorbed; blows are cushioned.
p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: All four verbs can describe softening the force of something, so the general meaning does not decide. Check which verb goes with “bill”.

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The paragraph before is mostly upbeat: mending pays, and repair cafés are spreading. The gapped sentence turns against that mood: “the boom is easy to overstate”. A turn is marked with “However”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, the boom is easy to overstate.” To overstate something is to make it sound bigger than it is.

steps.title: Compare with what came before
steps.text: The paragraph before is mostly positive: a mended coat passed on “can return more” than one “bought new and soon binned”, and volunteer cafés “have spread from town to town”. The gapped sentence warns that this success is easy to exaggerate, so it turns against the mood.

steps.title: Check the connectives
steps.text: “Moreover” adds a point in the same direction, “Thereafter” means after that in time, and “Namely” introduces the details of something just mentioned. Only “However” marks a turn.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “However, the boom is easy to overstate” turns from praise to caution. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Moreover” is a common formal linking word, and the text keeps adding points.
distractors.why_wrong: “Moreover” adds a point that goes the same way as the ones before. This sentence goes the other way: after the good news, it warns that the boom is easy to overstate (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text moves through the boom in order, so a time word can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: “Thereafter” means after that in time. The sentence is not about a later event but about how to judge the boom (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The rest of this paragraph gives details, and “Namely” introduces details.
distractors.why_wrong: “Namely” introduces the details of something just mentioned, as in a list. Nothing just mentioned is spelled out here; the sentence changes direction instead (step 2).

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: For a connective that opens a paragraph, compare the mood of the paragraph before with the sentence after the gap. A change from praise to warning calls for a contrast word.
p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not judge a connective by how formal it sounds. “Moreover” and “However” both sound formal, but they point in opposite directions.

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Almén warns that most of the platforms’ turnover rests on a thin seam of valuable goods and that two of the six would start losing money once their grants ran out. A revival that could break so easily is “fragile”. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the revival is a good deal more ___ than the applause admits”. “Than the applause admits” means that the gap names a weakness that the cheering leaves out.

steps.title: Use the evidence
steps.text: Almén points out that most of their turnover “still rests on a thin seam of high-value goods” and that two of the six platforms “would slip into the red the moment their start-up grants expired”. To slip into the red is to start losing money. A revival that rests on so little is fragile: easily broken.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Agile” means quick and flexible, which is praise. “Mercantile” means to do with trade, which describes the kind of business, not how secure it is. “Futile” means pointless, which goes too far: the text says that the boom is easy to overstate, not that it is pointless.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “A good deal more fragile than the applause admits” fits the warning. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The boom is fast-growing, and “agile” is a positive word often used about new businesses.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence names something the applause leaves out, so the word must be negative. “Agile” is praise, and the evidence after the gap is about weakness (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text is about trade, and “mercantile” means to do with trade.
distractors.why_wrong: “Mercantile” describes the kind of activity, not how secure it is. Almén’s evidence is about weakness – platforms that would “slip into the red” – so the gap needs a word for weakness (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Futile” is negative, like the warning, and it sounds like the strong word a critic would choose.
distractors.why_wrong: “Futile” means pointless. The text says that the boom is easy to overstate, not that it is pointless, and the danger Almén points to is that some platforms depend on grants. That is fragility (step 2).

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a gap is followed by “than the applause admits” or a similar phrase, the gap names the hidden problem. Pick the word that matches the size of the problem that the evidence shows.
p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: “Futile” has the right negative tone but the wrong strength. A revival can be shaky without being pointless, so check how strong the evidence is.

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Almén says that the work of mending is missing from the official statistics: it is “recorded in neither wages nor national accounts”. The idiom for something a system fails to record is “slip through the cracks”. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The labour of mending, she adds, slips through the ___ of the official statistics, recorded in neither wages nor national accounts.”

steps.title: Find the idiom
steps.text: The last part explains the gap: the work is “recorded in neither wages nor national accounts”, so the statistics miss it. English says that something unnoticed or unrecorded slips through the cracks, and here it “slips through the cracks of the official statistics”.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
