steps.text: “Fissures” and “fractures” are breaks, as in rock or bone, and “seams” are the lines where pieces of cloth are sewn together. They all name gaps or joins, but only “cracks” forms the idiom.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Slips through the cracks of the official statistics” – the statistics miss the work. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A fissure is a gap, and the statistics have a gap in them.
distractors.why_wrong: The idiom uses “cracks”, not “fissures”. A fissure is a long, deep split, usually in rock, and “slips through the fissures” is not an idiom (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph has just used “seam” in “a thin seam of high-value goods”, and things can come apart at the seams.
distractors.why_wrong: “Come apart at the seams” is a real idiom, but it means to fall apart, and there is no idiom “slip through the seams”. The idiom for going unrecorded is “slip through the cracks” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A fracture is a break, and statistics with a break in them would miss things.
distractors.why_wrong: Fractures are breaks, as in a bone. The idiom for something a system fails to record is “slip through the cracks” (step 2).

p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When a gap sits inside a familiar verb phrase – here “slips through the ___” – think of the fixed expression first, then check that it fits the meaning of the sentence.
p5-elf-b4-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: The four nouns all name lines, gaps or breaks, so meaning alone cannot decide. Only one of them completes the idiom.

p5-elf-b4-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Marris expected total sleep to decide how alert the cleaners felt, but the data suggested something else: what set the steadiest performers apart was how soon after waking they met bright light. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what Marris’s data suggested about afternoon alertness. “According to the text” means that the answer is stated in the text.

steps.title: Find the finding
steps.text: “The cleaners who logged the most hours in bed were not reliably the most alert; what set the steadiest performers apart, her data suggested, was how soon after waking they met a dose of bright light”.

steps.title: Note the detail
steps.text: Those who met bright light within the first hour “tended to sag less in the afternoon slump, even when their nights had been short”. So, in Marris’s data, the timing of light seemed to matter more than the length of sleep.

steps.title: Note the caution
steps.text: Marris calls it “a pattern in one workforce, not a prescription for everyone”, and says that a cleaner’s commute and coffee habits “could easily muddy the signal”. These are cautions about the finding, not the finding itself.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches the finding. In A, “tracked” means went together with: the sooner a cleaner met bright light, the more alert that cleaner tended to be, and this link was closer than the link with hours of sleep. B reverses it, C turns a possible distortion – coffee – into the cause, and D limits the benefit to long sleepers, although it held even after short nights.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Marris’s data suggested that how soon a cleaner met bright light tracked afternoon alertness better than how long they had slept. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Sleep is the usual explanation for feeling alert, and it was what Marris expected at first.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that the longest sleepers “were not reliably the most alert” (step 2). “Consistently the sharpest” is the opposite of the finding.

distractors.why_tempting: Coffee is mentioned in the text, and it is a well-known way to stay alert.
distractors.why_wrong: Coffee comes up only as something that “could easily muddy the signal” (step 4): a factor that might distort the result, not the pattern the data pointed to.

distractors.why_tempting: It sounds reasonable that light would help most when sleep was also good.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the benefit held “even when their nights had been short” (step 3). D limits it to long sleepers, which contradicts this.

p5-elf-b4-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text reports a finding and then adds cautions, keep the two apart. The answer to “what did Marris's data suggest” is the finding; the cautions are there to limit it.
p5-elf-b4-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Factors that a researcher names as possible distortions, such as coffee here, are easy to mistake for findings. Check what role the text gives each factor.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text grants that recycled glass saves real fuel, then shows that dirty recycled glass causes flaws that win back much of that saving once it makes up too much of the batch. Its verdict: what matters is how clean the glass is, not how full the batch is. C sums this up. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks for the point of the whole text, so the right answer must cover the turn in the argument, not just one result.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph gives the usual pitch – the more recycled glass, or cullet, in the furnace, the greener the bottle – and asks what happens when that glass is not clean. The second shows the fuel saving, the third the rising reject rate with dirty glass, the fourth Feld’s and Brandt’s views, and the fifth the writer’s verdict.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The last paragraph says that more cullet and greener glass “hold together only while the glass going in stays clean”, and sums up: “The number that matters, in the end, is not how full the batch is. It is how clean.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C has both halves: the real saving and the limit set by dirty glass. A gives only the opening mechanism, B gives advice that the text never offers, and D gives one step in the argument.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about why recycled glass stays the greener choice only while it is clean enough. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A is true: the first paragraph explains that cullet melts at a lower temperature and so ought to trim the fuel a furnace burns, and the trial confirmed the saving.
distractors.why_wrong: A is only the starting point. The rest of the text shows its limit: with dirty glass, once cullet passes about sixty percent, the reject rate climbs sharply, and “remelting the rejects handed back much of the fuel the cullet had saved”.

distractors.why_tempting: The trial used colour-sorted glass, and sorting sounds like the obvious fix for dirty glass.
distractors.why_wrong: No one in the text says that glass should be sorted by colour, and the writer gives recycling schemes no advice. The text reports what clean and dirty glass did in the furnace, and Brandt warns that cleaning the stream works “only so far and never for free”.

distractors.why_tempting: D describes a real mechanism from the third paragraph: flawed glass is pulled and melted a second time.
distractors.why_wrong: That is one step on the way to the verdict, not the main point. The text is about when recycled glass stays the greener choice, and D says nothing about the fuel saving or its limit (step 3).

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions in a text that tests a popular claim, the answer is usually the tested, corrected version of the claim. Look for the sentence that sums up – here “The number that matters, in the end …”.
p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Options that are true but partial are the main trap here. A gives only the pitch and D only one step of the problem; C is the only option that joins the saving and its limit.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The fuel meters showed that each added tenth of cullet cut fuel use by roughly three percent, “clean stream or dirty, right across the range they tested”. A gives the figure and the clean-or-dirty point. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about fuel use. Fuel is covered in the second paragraph; the reject rate, which is a different measure, comes in the third.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “On energy the result was just as advertised, and pleasingly straight: each added tenth of cullet cut the furnace's fuel use by roughly three percent, clean stream or dirty, right across the range they tested.”

steps.title: Note the limits
steps.text: “Roughly” makes the figure approximate, and “right across the range they tested” limits the result to the amounts that were tried. On the fuel meters, the saving did not depend on whether the glass was clean.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches. B makes the saving grow without any limit, C gives the fuel saving a clean-or-dirty difference that belongs to the reject rate, and D gives a reason for the saving that the text does not give.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Each added tenth of cullet cut fuel use by about three percent, with clean or dirty glass. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: B keeps the three-percent figure, and the saving held across the whole test.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says “roughly three percent”, not an exact figure, and the saving held only “right across the range they tested” (step 3). Nothing says that the savings would go on growing without any limit.

distractors.why_tempting: Clean versus dirty glass is the main contrast of the text, so it is easy to apply it to the fuel too.
distractors.why_wrong: For fuel, the text says the saving came “clean stream or dirty” (step 2). The difference between the streams showed up in the reject rate, not on the fuel meters.

distractors.why_tempting: Recycling is often linked with lower carbon, and the first paragraph mentions the carbon a furnace breathes out.
distractors.why_wrong: The text explains the saving by the lower melting temperature of cullet, not by carbon locked inside the glass. Carbon is mentioned only as something the furnace gives off.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a text measures two things – here fuel and rejects – make sure each option talks about the right one. A contrast that holds for one measure may not hold for the other.
p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: An absolute phrase such as “without any limit” goes beyond “right across the range they tested”. Keep the text’s limits.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: With the mixed municipal cullet, the reject rate “edged up slowly at first and then, once cullet passed about sixty percent, climbed sharply”. D describes this two-stage rise. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks about the reject rate with the mixed municipal cullet only. The text gives a different result for clean cullet, so keep the two apart.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “With the mixed municipal stream it edged up slowly at first and then, once cullet passed about sixty percent, climbed sharply”.

steps.title: See why
steps.text: Municipal cullet carries bits of ceramic and stone that do not melt at the temperature glass does, so they stay in the glass as “stones”. The flawed glass has to be melted again, and that costs fuel: “remelting the rejects handed back much of the fuel the cullet had saved”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches. A is what happened with clean cullet, B makes the rise sudden from the start, and C describes a fall that the text never reports.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: With municipal cullet the reject rate rose slowly at first and then sharply above about sixty percent. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A is in the text almost word for word.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes the clean, sorted cullet: “With clean, sorted cullet the reject rate barely stirred”. The question asks about the mixed municipal stream (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Dirty glass caused the problems, so it can seem that it caused them at once.
distractors.why_wrong: The rate “edged up slowly at first” (step 2). It climbed sharply only once cullet passed about sixty percent of the batch.

distractors.why_tempting: Caps and crockery are named in the text, and screening them out sounds like a sensible improvement.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the operators screened anything out or that the rate fell. It rose (step 2).

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question names one of two groups – here the municipal stream – find the sentence about that group and check its shape: how the result changed and where it turned.
p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: A wrong option may be a real sentence from the text about the other group. Check which group each sentence describes.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The flaws come from bits of ceramic and stone that arrive with the municipal cullet, and “each further ton of dirty glass carried its fixed freight of stones”. Clean cullet had been picked clean of everything but glass, so it can fill most of the batch, while more dirty cullet means more stones. B states this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Imply” means that the text does not state the reason directly. Put together what it says about the flaws and about the two kinds of cullet.

steps.title: Find where the flaws come from
steps.text: “Municipal cullet carries a small, stubborn load of things that are not glass — a chip of ceramic, a shard of stoneware, a fleck of stone off the roadside — and these do not melt at the temperature glass does.” They become “stones”, hard bits in the glass that seed cracks.

steps.title: Link the flaws to the amount
steps.text: The text adds that “each further ton of dirty glass carried its fixed freight of stones”. The clean cullet had been “picked clean of everything but glass”, and with it “the reject rate barely stirred, even when cullet ran most of the batch”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B draws exactly that link. A claims a difference in fuel saving that the text denies, C says that municipal glass can never be cleaned enough, and D names the colour sorting, although the text ties the flaws to things that are not glass.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The stones come in with the dirty glass, so the more dirty cullet, the more flaws. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: It sounds natural that purer glass would melt more easily and save more fuel.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that each added tenth of cullet cut fuel use by about the same amount, “clean stream or dirty”. On the fuel meters the two streams did not differ; the difference lay in the flaws.

distractors.why_tempting: Brandt knows of no municipal system that delivers glass clean enough for the very top of the range, which can sound like “never”.
distractors.why_wrong: Brandt says that the stream “can indeed be cleaned”, though “only so far and never for free”: the last chips are “the hardest and dearest to pick out”, which means costly, not impossible. The doubt is only about running at “the very top of the range”. “Never … under any circumstances whatever” is far stronger.

distractors.why_tempting: D is true: the clean cullet was sorted by colour, and the municipal stream was not sorted.
distractors.why_wrong: True, but it names the wrong difference. The flaws come from things that are not glass – ceramic, stoneware, stone – and the clean cullet had been “picked clean of everything but glass” (step 3). The colour of the glass is not what makes the stones.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “imply … why” questions, follow the cause through the text step by step: where the problem comes from, and how it grows. The right answer states the link that the text leaves you to draw.
p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: A true fact is not always the reason. D is correct that the clean cullet was sorted by colour, but the flaws come from bits that are not glass, so colour is the wrong difference.

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer says the season’s record is “more divided than Feld's rule allows”: the fuel savings are real, but past a certain point, on the mixed stream that most works receive, the stones win back what the furnace saved. Accepting the saving but limiting Feld’s rule – that is B. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Feld’s claim that a furnace can never hold too much cullet. Keep the writer’s voice apart from Feld’s and Brandt’s.

steps.title: Find Feld’s claim
steps.text: Feld says: “Fill every furnace to the top with cullet — always, on every batch.” And: “There is no such thing as too much recycled glass.”

steps.title: Find the writer’s answer
steps.text: The last paragraph begins: “The season's record, read whole, is more divided than Feld's rule allows.” It grants that “the fuel savings are real”, but adds that more cullet stays greener “only while the glass going in stays clean”; past that point, on the mixed stream, “the stones win back what the furnace saved”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches: real savings, but too much dirty cullet backfires. “Qualified” here means accepted only in part, and “backfires” means has the opposite effect from the one intended. A puts the writer on Feld’s side, C gives the writer Feld’s certainty, and D says that the saving is too small to matter, which the writer denies.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer qualifies Feld’s claim: the fuel saving is real, but adding more cullet stays greener only while the glass is clean. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: A sounds as careful as the right answer, and the text does discuss cleaning the glass.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer treats contamination as the limit that matters: a furnace fed the worst cullet “has a ceiling, and it sits lower than the collection targets like to admit”, and the mixed stream is what “most works actually receive”. That is no minor snag.

distractors.why_tempting: Feld’s words are the most confident in the text and easy to remember.
distractors.why_wrong: That certainty is Feld’s. The writer says that the record “is more divided than Feld's rule allows” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does criticise Feld’s rule and the collection targets, so a negative view of cullet can seem to follow.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says that the record “does not show that cullet is a false economy” – a saving that ends up costing more than it gives – and that “the fuel savings are real” (step 3).

p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, look for a sentence where the writer weighs a claim, such as “more divided than … allows”. It usually means that the writer accepts part of the claim and rejects the rest.
p5-elf-b5-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Two options can sound equally careful. A and B are both moderate in tone, so decide by direction: does the writer side with Feld, or limit Feld’s rule?
